newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO begin patching up security relations.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO begin patching up security relations.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian security forces have begun patching up a violence-scarred relationship ahead of U.S.-mediated talks which a U.N. peace negotiator says have little chance of achieving quick results.

The Israeli army said top officers in the Gaza Strip had toured the area with Palestinian police commanders to try to ease tensions. Just last week, Israeli soldiers and Palestinian policemen were shooting at one another.

"To reduce...friction and prevent another escalation of (violence), they agreed on and marked security areas of about 300 metres where Palestinian police will prevent the entry of demonstrators," an Israeli army spokeswoman said.
A Palestinian security official, Brigadier General Zyad al-Atrash, denied any "no-go" zones had been set up but said there had been agreement on "coordination to calm things down".

Clashes triggered by Israel's opening on September 24 of a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem claimed 73 Arab and Jewish lives, the worst Israeli-Palestinian violence since a 1993 peace deal.

Joint Israeli-Palestinian patrols, part of three years of U.S.-nurtured peace deals, have ground to a halt in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, in areas where Jewish settlements and Israeli soldiers remain pending a final accord.

But a PLO security official in Jenin said on Friday joint patrols would resume in the West Bank town on Sunday. He said he had been informed by an Israeli military liaison officer that an Israeli closure around Jenin had been lifted.
The Israeli army had no immediate comment. Israeli travel restrictions on Palestinians moving between other towns in the West Bank remained in effect.

On the diplomatic front, U.S. President Bill Clinton said Secretary of State Warren Christopher would go to the Middle East this weekend as Israel and the PLO prepared for a resumption of talks on Sunday at the Erez crossing in Gaza.

The Erez talks, mediated by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, will focus on Israel's long-delayed troop redeployment from the West Bank city of Hebron, where some 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Palestinians.

Agreement to hold the sessions was reached at a two-day emergency White House summit this week attended by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein.
Christopher will hold separate talks with Netanyahu and Arafat but it is unclear whether he will attend the Erez session, State Department sources said.
U.N. envoy Terje Larsen, who helped broker the original Israel-PLO self-rule deal and has been mediating again between them, said he doubted vital issues would be resolved quickly.

Netanyahu is seeking security modifications to the accord on a partial pullout in Hebron which the previous Labour-led government signed with the PLO. Palestinians say they will not renegotiate its terms.

"Let me put it this way -- I don't think it is very likely that they will be able to find a solution to the vital questions until a bit into November, and as you know the American presidential elections are on November 5," Larsen said in Oslo.
Larsen leaves for Israel on Sunday with Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal.
In Paris, Arafat met French President Jacques Chirac and called for a European presence at the negotiations.
Chirac telephoned Netanyahu to brief him on his talks with Arafat but did not mention the Palestinian leader's suggestion, Chirac's spokeswoman said.
Israel has been cool to a European role, which has traditionally been seen in the Jewish state as pro-Arab.
It has also been locked in a dispute with the European Union over a proposed visit by a troika of European foreign ministers to Orient House, the PLO's headquarters in East Jerusalem.
